content: Closed suction drainage systems are commonly utilized in surgical settings to remove fluids, particularly blood, from wounds following surgery. The primary purpose of these systems is to minimize the risk of wound hematomas and infections. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of closed suction drainage systems specifically in the context of orthopedic surgeries. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted. This included the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group Specialised Register (as of March 2006) and communication with the Cochrane Wounds Group. Additional searches were performed in the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (Cochrane Library, 2006, Issue 1) and MEDLINE, covering publications from 1966 to March 2006. Articles in all languages were considered for inclusion. The selection criteria focused on randomized or quasi-randomized trials that compared the use of closed suction drainage systems to no drainage systems in both elective and emergency orthopedic surgeries. Two independent authors evaluated the quality of the trials using a nine-item scale and extracted relevant data. When appropriate, results from comparable studies were combined for analysis. A total of 36 studies were identified, involving 5,464 participants and 5,697 surgical wounds. The types of surgeries included in these studies were hip and knee replacements, shoulder surgeries, hip fracture surgeries, spinal surgeries, cruciate ligament reconstructions, open meniscectomies, and fracture fixation surgeries. The pooled results from these studies showed no statistically significant differences in the rates of wound infection, hematoma formation, wound dehiscence, or the need for re-operations between patients who had closed suction drains and those who did not. However, patients with closed suction drains were more likely to require blood transfusions. On the other hand, patients without drains experienced a higher frequency of wound dressing reinforcement and bruising. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence from randomized trials to recommend the routine use of closed suction drainage systems in orthopedic surgeries. They emphasized the need for further randomized trials with larger sample sizes across various types of orthopedic procedures to draw definitive conclusions.
